passage: At the preschool's free-play hour, Indu hid behind the classroom door, and Pema, the seeker, opened the door and spotted Indu within seconds. Next round Indu tried the curtain by the window and lasted a little longer. The round after that, Indu wriggled under a nap-room cot and stayed hidden until the teacher clapped for a snack. Pema looked in three places before giving up.

qa.q: Where did Indu hide in the first round?
qa.a: Indu hid behind the classroom door.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling when Pema gave up looking?
qa.a: Indu was probably delighted and proud, because the third hiding place finally worked after two failures.

qa.q: What other approach could Indu use to hide well, and why?
qa.a: Indu could watch which places Pema checks first and pick a spot that Pema tends to skip, because the seeker's habits tell which places are safe. 😊

qa.q: How does Pema see the third round?
qa.a: Pema is puzzled and probably a little frustrated after checking three places without success, and may want a turn to hide next.

grounding: After being found in seconds behind the door, a child tries the curtain, then a cot, and each round teaches which spots work.

passage: I'm Neelam, Jyoti's neighbour, and we played hide-and-seek in her flat on Sunday. Round one, Jyoti hid behind the door, and I found her before I'd finished counting in my head. Round two, she went behind the long curtain; her toes gave her away, but it took me longer. Round three, she was under the bed, flat as a mat, and I gave up. I don't know if she planned it, but each hiding place got better.

qa.q: Where did Jyoti hide in round three?
qa.a: She was under the bed, flat as a mat.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling when she gave up in round three?
qa.a: Neelam was surprised and impressed, noticing that each hiding place got better.

qa.q: What else could Jyoti try to hide even better?
qa.a: She could think about where Neelam searched last time and pick somewhere Neelam hasn't looked yet.

qa.q: What might Jyoti be feeling after winning round three?
qa.a: She is probably delighted and proud after being found fast twice.

grounding: An observer describes a child who is found quickly behind the door, then tries the curtain and the bed, learning which spots work.

passage:
Monday: Dhruv hid behind the bedroom door. Sunaina found him before she reached ten. He groaned.
Tuesday: he picked the curtain. Sunaina walked past twice before seeing his feet. "Almost!"
Thursday: he slid under the bed and held still. Sunaina searched the door, the curtain, and gave up. Dhruv crawled out, dusty and grinning. "The bed's the best."

qa.q: Where did Dhruv hide on Tuesday?
What was Dhruv feeling when he crawled out on Thursday?
qa.a: He was proud and happy that the bed finally worked.

qa.q: What else could Dhruv try next time Sunaina seeks?
qa.a: He could pick a new spot again, since Sunaina may now check under the bed first.

qa.q: How does the change look to Sunaina?
qa.a: Sunaina finds Dhruv harder to find each day and may feel a bit frustrated and impressed.

grounding: Over several days a child moves from the door to the curtain to under the bed, learning from being found which spots work.
